questions.question: DPO's key insight is that the RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy. What does this allow?
options: The policy can be trained without any human preference data
The reward model can be eliminated and the policy optimized directly using the preference data
The KL penalty can be set to zero without causing reward hacking
The reference policy can be continuously updated during training
questions.explanation: Rafailov et al. showed the RLHF optimum has a closed form in terms of the policy-to-reference ratio. Substituting this into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood and letting the partition function Z(x) cancel yields a loss in policy parameters alone — no reward model needed.

questions.question: What is the 'Degraded Chosen Response' phenomenon in DPO?
options: The chosen response's absolute log-probability increases faster than the rejected response's
The reward model assigns a higher score to the rejected response after training
DPO can push the chosen response's absolute log-probability down as long as the rejected response falls even faster
The model forgets the chosen response format during extended training
questions.explanation: DPO's loss only constrains the relative gap between chosen and rejected log-probs. It can decrease the chosen response's absolute log-probability as long as the rejected falls faster, resulting in a model that has learned the ranking but assigns lower probability to the correct response.

questions.question: KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization) is designed to address which specific limitation of DPO?
options: DPO requires white-box access to the model's activations
DPO requires paired preference data; KTO works with single labeled outputs using binary desirable/undesirable signals
DPO cannot handle tasks with more than two possible responses
DPO's training is unstable when the reference policy is far from optimal
questions.explanation: KTO drops the pairwise structure entirely. Instead of requiring (chosen, rejected) pairs, it accepts single outputs labeled as desirable or undesirable, mapping to a prospect-theory utility. Unpaired feedback data is far more plentiful in practice.

questions.question: SimPO addresses DPO's length exploitation by:
options: Adding a penalty term proportional to the difference in sequence lengths between chosen and rejected
Removing the reference policy and normalizing log-likelihood by sequence length with a margin
Training the reward model to be length-invariant using data augmentation
Using byte-pair encoding instead of token-level probability for length normalization
questions.explanation: SimPO removes the reference policy and uses (beta / |y|) * log pi(y|x) — length-normalized log-likelihood plus a margin gamma. DPO's length bias arises because longer chosen responses produce larger log-prob gaps by construction; length normalization removes this incentive.

questions.question: ORPO's key architectural difference from DPO is:
options: ORPO uses a larger reference model than the policy being trained
ORPO trains from a base model in one stage by adding an odds-ratio term to the standard SFT NLL loss, eliminating the need for a separate SFT checkpoint
ORPO replaces the preference optimization objective with a contrastive loss
ORPO requires a separate critic model to estimate the policy's value function
questions.explanation: ORPO adds a preference term (log odds-ratio of chosen over rejected) directly to the standard SFT negative log-likelihood. The SFT loss acts as its own regularizer, allowing training from a base model in a single stage without needing a separate SFT reference checkpoint.

questions.question: Rafailov et al. (NeurIPS 2024) proved that Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) like DPO:
options: Completely avoid reward hacking because they have no explicit reward model to over-optimize
Still exhibit the same Gao et al. peak-and-collapse over-optimization curve, just with the implicit reward ratio instead of an explicit RM
Are immune to Goodhart's Law when the preference data is sufficiently large
Achieve lower gold-reward than standard RLHF at matched KL budgets
questions.explanation: Rafailov et al. (NeurIPS 2024) demonstrated that DPO, IPO, and SLiC show the same peak-and-collapse shape on gold-reward-vs-KL curves. DAAs do not escape Goodhart; they shift where it bites from 'reward model over-optimized' to 'reference policy ratio over-optimized.'
